newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Peace envoy says Sierra Leone returning to normal.
newsitem.headline: Peace envoy says Sierra Leone returning to normal.

text.p: A Ghanaian minister involved in talks to bring a return to democracy in Sierra Leone after the May 25 coup said on Sunday that life was beginning to return to normal in the capital Freetown.

"Whilst in Freetown, we have been able to visit areas in the capital and we saw normal life returning, with businesses starting working," Ghana's deputy foreign minister, James Victor Gbeho, told a news conference.
"We never saw any act of violence, or any dead bodies around, as being reported in the international press," he added.
Gbeho and his delegation finished three days of talks with coup leader Johnny Paul Koroma and other military leaders on Saturday.

"Ghana still supports the OAU (Organisation of African Unity) decision reached in Harare recently, calling on all countries to do their utmost to restore the constitutional order in Sierra Leone," Gbeho told Reuters late on Saturday.
"We believe that the best way to resolve the crisis is by diplomatic means, to reach a negotiated settlement, rather than by fighting," he added.

In a brief declaration to reporters after the talks ended, Koroma, installed as head of state last week, said: "We hope that the task that Ghana has undertaken together with us will finally lead to bringing about the restoration of peace, security and constitutional order."

The military government wants the former rebels of the Revolutionary United Front, who rallied to the coup, to be given a role in any new government, but is adamant that ousted president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah should not return.
However, Gbeho said the coup leaders wanted a negotiated settlement. "They see our presence here as a window of opportunity and they are ready for talks," he said.

He declined to reveal the substance of the talks with Koroma, but sources said coup leaders had discussed the idea of staying in power for only seven or eight months, rather than the two years they had announced, if a peace-keeping force other than the ECOMOG force already in the country is deployed.
The West African ECOMOG force is led by Nigeria, whose gunboats bombarded Freetown on June 2 in a failed effort to reverse the coup.

An anticipated further attack from the Nigerian troops never came, but the coup leaders have accused Nigeria of arming Kamajor traditional hunters in the east of the country and encouraging them to oppose the military regime.
Gbeho told the news conference that if such a move had happened, it had nothing to do with ECOMOG.
"I would like to say that has not been approved by ECOWAS (Economic Community of West African States) leaders, so if it has happened, it is not an ECOMOG involvement," he told the news conference.
